Opioids.note: HSE bullet read in full: "ask someone to stay with you or phone someone you trust - make sure that you are not alone" (first bullet after "If you have a challenging experience, you could:"). Both The Level pages: "If you are able, call and talk to somebody you trust and ask them to help keep you calm." The line says no more than these.

The Level (heroin): "Do not take more heroin, alcohol, or other drugs, as these can make you feel worse."; same sentence with "opioids" on the prescription opioids page. HSE opioids page (the www2 address given opened as given; H1 "Reducing risks from opioids - Opioids") has the quoted sentence first under "Mixing opioids with alcohol or other drugs".

The Level (heroin): "Move to somewhere quiet - try to sit or lie down and do something relaxing." The line keeps only "sit", which is less than the sources say, not more. For the editor: the same HSE list also says "Avoid going somewhere else by yourself." and "Stay in a safe environment with other people if you can."; line 0 of this family already covers not being alone, so keep line 0 above this one.

The Level (heroin): "Focus on breathing - try taking slow, deep breaths."; prescription opioids page: "Focus on breathing try taking slow and deep breaths."; HSE bullet: "pick something else to focus on - for example, your breathing or talk about something you enjoy doing".
The line keeps the HSE's manner ("in small sips"); the HSE's amount is "a glass of water", which the line gives as "some water". Neither source gives any other limit for this family.

Last line of the family, as required. NHS box "Immediate action required: Call 999 if:" with the lead-in "You take more than your prescribed dose of methadone and you:" and the two bullets "feel very drowsy" and "find it difficult to breathe": the line keeps both terms. HSE (112 or 999) and The Level (111) confirm the breathing sign. For the editor: "very drowsy" as a reason to call emergency services rests on the NHS methadone page alone; The Level sends "having trouble staying awake" (heroin) and "feeling extremely drowsy" (prescription opioids) to "a doctor or Healthline" and keeps 111 for "unable to wake up" / "unable to stay awake". The line errs toward calling, so it stays.

Stimulants.note: The quoted sentence is the first one under "What to do if someone is overamping?" on The Level's story about stimulants (MDMA, meth, coke), dated December 12th, 2024. The line keeps both of the source's hedges ("mild", "can") and says it for the family the source says it for. One publisher only. For the editor: the same section's water advice, written for helpers, is "Give them some water or a sweet drink to sip slowly."
The Level (amphetamine and methamphetamine pages, "Try:" lists): "Move to somewhere quiet – try to sit or lie down and do something relaxing."

The Level (amphetamine and cocaine pages): "Focus on breathing – try taking slow, deep breaths."; HSE bullet: "pick something else to focus on - for example, your breathing or talk about something you enjoy doing".

HSE: "ask someone to stay with you or phone someone you trust - make sure that you are not alone"; The Level (methamphetamine and cocaine pages): "If you are able, call and talk to somebody you trust and ask them to help keep you calm."

All three passages are advice for before and during use (ADF "Reducing harm"; HSE advice to event attendees; DanceSafe "Basic Tips" under "PREVENTING HEATSTROKE"), not advice written for the moment it is already too much; the act is the same and the line adds nothing to it. The HSE bullet in full: "Keep cool and stay hydrated but don’t drink over a pint of water an hour. Take breaks from dancing, check in with yourself and others." DanceSafe's sentence about drugs ("Certain drugs can increase your risk of heatstroke by:") stands under the heading "Heatstroke is surprisingly dangerous". The wording is close to DanceSafe's sentence but is not a copy.

The Level (amphetamine): "Do not take more speed, caffeine, alcohol or other drugs, as these can make you feel worse."; same sentence with "meth" on the methamphetamine page. HSE: "Do not take any other drugs - it can make the experience worse." (last sentence under "If you have a challenging experience").

Last line of the family, as required. All four signs are in The Level's own list under "Call 111 if someone:" ("Has a very high temperature (they may be sweating)", "Has difficulty breathing", "Has chest pains", "Has a seizure, convulsions or tremors"). "Call an ambulance" is the ADF's own term ("Call triple zero (000) and request an ambulance if you or someone else has any of the following symptoms"); in the ADF list the chest-pain bullet stands under "heart attack symptoms such as:". NHS lead-in as read: "You take more than your prescribed dose of methylphenaidate and:" (the spelling is the page's or the reading tool's).
